card.hook: Picture a huge white mosque and its twin upside down in the water, and you standing there thinking, 'Is that real?' On a still evening at Wahat Al Karama, it is.
card.stand_here: Stand in Wahat Al Karama, beside the central circular reflecting pool on the memorial plaza, and face south-west toward the mosque across the motorway. Crouch low near the water's edge so the reflection fills the bottom half of your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pool, the plaza and the whole mosque in. Then try 1x for a cleaner view, and 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the domes and minarets closer, because the mosque is a fair way off across the road.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mosque, then slide it a little darker so the white marble keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Arrive about two hours before sunset to grab a good spot for blue hour. One guide says 30 minutes before sunset works for both daylight and lit-up shots, and the mosque's night lighting follows the phases of the moon. Haze is common, so a slightly soft skyline is normal, and clearer evenings give crisper reflections.
card.selfie_here: Inside the grounds, try the reflecting pool near the entrance: use the front camera and stand so the mosque is behind you, with the water as your mirrored backdrop. The roped-off sections under the arches around the courtyard are good for selfies with the arches behind you and fewer people in the frame. Try 0.5x to squeeze more of the mosque in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the memorial plaza beside the circular pool, ask a passer-by to stand where the mosque and you both fit in the frame, while you stand by the pool with the mosque behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: A busy motorway separates the park from the mosque, so don't cross it on foot; take a taxi, the free shuttle or the pedestrian bridge. Drones are prohibited, and always ask before photographing a worshipper or anyone else. The mosque is a place of worship with a modest dress code and its own visiting and photo rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the mosque and its reflection in one shot, with the gridline running right along the water's edge so the two halves match like a pair of socks.
card.good_to_know: The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is the largest mosque in the United Arab Emirates. It was built between 1994 and 2007 and opened in December 2007. It has 82 domes, four minarets of about 107 m, and a marble courtyard with floral inlay covering about 17,000 square metres.

card.hook: A dome that weighs about 7,000 tonnes and still looks like it's floating? Yes, that's the Louvre Abu Dhabi, and it's a show-off in the best way. Skip the crowd under it for a minute and grab a calmer view first.
card.stand_here: Head to Aptitude Cafe, just north-east of the museum building, and sit or stand in the outdoor seating area. Face the museum so the dome and waterfront sit behind the terrace.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the terrace, dome and waterfront all squeeze in. Then try 1x for a cleaner look at the museum. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for a tighter shot of the dome and its pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the dome on the upper line and let the tables and chairs fill the bottom third, then tap the dome and slide it a touch darker so the white stays crisp against the sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light on the dome. The light changes with the season, so have a quick look on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the outdoor seating area of Aptitude Cafe, right in front of the museum, where posing with the Louvre behind you is a popular shot. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone offers it) and tuck the dome over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the waterfront promenade across the museum lagoon, facing the museum, so the whole building and the dome low over the water fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The cafe terrace is part of a commercial venue, and the dome area and galleries may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the dome in the top half and a tabletop in the bottom half, with your coffee as the co-star?
card.good_to_know: The museum was designed by Jean Nouvel, and its white dome rests on four concrete pillars. It's the largest art museum on the Arabian Peninsula. Under an agreement between the UAE and France signed in 2007, it can use the Louvre name until 2047.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Aptitude Cafe, just north-east of the museum building, and sit or stand in the outdoor seating area. Face the museum so the dome and waterfront sit behind the terrace.

card.hook: From the public beach, Emirates Palace is a small sandy-coloured smudge on the shoreline, and honestly that's part of the charm. You get the whole Abu Dhabi skyline doubled in the water, with a palace tucked in.
card.stand_here: Stand on Corniche Beach, in the eastern section, with the water in front of you. The hotel is to the south-west, about 2.7 km away, or roughly 35 minutes on foot along the shore, so face south-west and look along the shoreline.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full skyline and the reflections, but the palace will look small. Tap 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to bring it closer. Save 0.5x for the hotel entrance, if you go, when you want the whole facade in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water along the bottom third with the skyline above it, and keep the horizon level so the reflections look natural.
card.best_time: A guide to Corniche Beach recommends sunrise from the east end of the Corniche. Get there early and the towers and the water should look their best.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the hotel and take your selfie on the grand staircase that climbs to the lobby, with the stairs behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little higher. For a palace-front backdrop outside, stand under the archways beside the entrance fountains.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the forecourt from the entrance fountains so the fountains and the facade fill the frame, while you pose near the fountains.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is private property with security staff, so dress modestly with knees and shoulders covered. Keep your photos handheld and quick, because security pays close attention to photographers. Photos are generally allowed inside but video isn't, according to user answers on a Q&A page. That isn't an official rule, so check the hotel's official site before you go. The public Corniche Beach has no photography restrictions.
card.challenge: Count the domes. You'll never reach 115 from the beach, but see how many you can fit in one zoomed-in shot.
card.good_to_know: Emirates Palace opened in 2005 and is now run as the Emirates Palace Mandarin Oriental. It has one central patterned dome and 114 smaller domes, and the design is so symmetrical that even a quick straight-on shot looks tidy. The hotel has its own 1.3 km beach, but it's private, so the public Corniche Beach is the one to use.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Corniche Beach, in the eastern section, with the water in front of you. The hotel is to the south-west, about 2.7 km away, or roughly 35 minutes on foot along the shore, so face south-west and look along the shoreline.

card.hook: Picture a big white palace sitting calmly on the Gulf shoreline, looking like a pale cut-out against the Abu Dhabi skyline. That's Qasr Al Watan from the Corniche, and it's one of the easiest buildings in the city to recognise.
card.stand_here: Stand on Corniche Road, toward the western end of the Corniche, where the palace stands by the shoreline. Face west: the palace is a good distance away, so it reads as a pale shape against the skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the Corniche, the water and the skyline. Then try 2x to 5x to bring the palace closer (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground, because it makes the palace very small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the palace on one of the vertical lines, keep the horizon level, then tap the palace and slide it a little darker so the white stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or evening usually gives softer light on the white stone. Light-show times are reported differently, so check the official site before you go, and if you stay after dark, use night mode and rest your phone against a railing or wall.
card.selfie_here: Inside the grounds, step into the golden calligraphy Power of Words sculpture for a different angle, and try to get the palace complex in view behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x, or stand in front of the white façade on the entrance side before you go in.
card.ask_someone: Ask them to stand on the plaza or lawn facing the front of the palace, with you in front of it, so the whole façade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Entering the grounds needs a ticket, so check the official site first. Don't photograph security personnel or systems. Selfie sticks are reported as banned without official accreditation, so check at the Visitor Centre. Keep your belongings with you.
card.challenge: Can you get the palace on a gridline with a dead-level horizon and nobody's head poking into the shot? Take a few, since haze and passers-by love to photobomb.
card.good_to_know: Qasr Al Watan is the presidential palace of the United Arab Emirates. The façade is white granite and limestone, and the central dome is 37 m across. It was finished in 2017 and opened to visitors on 11 March 2019, and it's still used for state receptions and government meetings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Corniche Road, toward the western end of the Corniche, where the palace stands by the shoreline. Face west: the palace is a good distance away, so it reads as a pale shape against the skyline.

card.hook: Imagine the whole Abu Dhabi waterfront laid out below you like a map, with the Corniche curling away and the Gulf glittering beyond it. That's the view from the top of Etihad Towers, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Go up to the Observation Deck at 300 in Tower 2 (74th floor) and stand at the west-facing windows. Face out toward the Corniche, Emirates Palace and the Gulf.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to grab the whole sweep of coast and city. Then try 1x for a natural look at the shoreline, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the palace or a stretch of beach.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the Corniche coastline along a lower grid line, so the water and city fill the frame.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon and stay into sunset. The sky changes colour, then the city lights come on below you.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie from outside, head to the Etihad Towers archway at the west end of the Corniche, or the sand at the west end of Corniche Beach. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the towers rise over your shoulder. Late afternoon light is best.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Corniche promenade facing the towers, a few steps back from the archway, while you stand at the archway so the whole group of towers fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Observation Deck at 300 is a ticketed indoor attraction, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find Emirates Palace from 74 floors up, then zoom in until it fills your frame like a postcard.
card.good_to_know: Etihad Towers is a group of five towers of different heights, holding offices, apartments and a hotel. Tower 2 is the tallest, at 74 floors and 305 metres. You may also recognise the complex from the 2015 film Furious 7.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the Observation Deck at 300 in Tower 2 (74th floor) and stand at the west-facing windows. Face out toward the Corniche, Emirates Palace and the Gulf.

card.hook: This glass tower is leaning on purpose, and it tilts more than three times as far as the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Your phone screen will be very happy about that.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open grounds of the Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre, next to the tower, and face west, because the tower is to the west of you. Stay back across the grounds instead of going right to the base, and if you can, drift north or south of the tower, where the lean shows more clearly.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower in one frame. If you end up close to the building, switch to 0.5x and keep your phone level, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the glass and the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the tower upright in the frame, then tap the tower and drag the slider a little darker so the sky stays blue and the glass keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon or around sunset, when the light picks out the glass. The tower is also lit at night, so use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the street-side view along Khaleej Al Arabi Street, beside the tower, which a guide calls the best angle to show the 18-degree tilt. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low so the whole tower leans over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the exhibition centre grounds so they can fit the whole tower in the frame while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: A guard post can restrict access right beside the tower, there's no public observation deck, and traffic on the road in front can spoil close shots, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the top and the bottom of the tower in one frame with a gridline running straight up the glass, then tilt your own body 18 degrees to match.
card.good_to_know: Capital Gate is designed to lean 18 degrees to the west, and in June 2010 Guinness World Records named it the farthest manmade leaning building. It's over 160 metres tall with 35 storeys and opened on 21 December 2011. Offices fill much of it, and the Andaz Hotel is on floors 18 to 33.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the open grounds of the Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre, next to the tower, and face west, because the tower is to the west of you. Stay back across the grounds instead of going right to the base, and if you can, drift north or south of the tower, where the lean shows more clearly.

card.hook: Picture a 1761 watchtower with glass skyscrapers peeking over its shoulder. That's Qasr Al Hosn, and the best trick here is letting the old stone frame the new city.
card.stand_here: Walk into the Qasr Al Hosn grounds and stand under one of the fort's arches, right on the phone icon on the map. Face out through the arch so the skyscrapers sit in the opening.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the skyscrapers framed by the arch. Switch to 0.5x to fit in more of the arch and courtyard, or try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the watchtower's stone walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the arch so its sides stay straight, then tap the skyscrapers and slide a bit darker so the bright sky doesn't turn the stonework into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when the low sun skims across the stone and shows off its texture. Midday light is harsher, so you may need to nudge the picture darker.
card.selfie_here: Stand beneath the coral and sea stone watchtower at the Inner Fort, the oldest part of the complex, with the tower behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the whole tower fits over your shoulder. For a moodier shot, stand in a doorway in the courtyard, look down, and let the peaceful courtyard fill the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't use flash inside, and selfie sticks may not be allowed, so check with the venue before you go. Bring sunglasses, because the glare from the white ground can strain your eyes.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the same arch, one step apart, and see which one gets the best mix of sky, skyline and old stone.
card.good_to_know: Qasr Al Hosn is the oldest stone building in Abu Dhabi city. It began in 1761 as a watchtower guarding the island's only freshwater well, and became a small fort and the Sheikh's home in 1793. It was painted white during renovations between 1976 and 1983, which is why it's called the White Fort, and it reopened as a museum and cultural site in 2018. Parts of it are ticketed and opening times vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into the Qasr Al Hosn grounds and stand under one of the fort's arches, right on the phone icon on the map. Face out through the arch so the skyscrapers sit in the opening.

card.hook: Picture yourself crouched on the floor, phone almost touching the ground, and a thin ribbon of water pointing straight at a wall of timber pillars. It looks a bit silly, and it's the best picture on this site.
card.stand_here: Stand in The Forum, right beside the water channel that runs across the floor. Face along the channel towards the timber pillars of the church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to stretch the channel and pillars into bold lines. Switch to 1x for a calmer, tidier shot, then try 2x to 5x to pick out one detail, like a screen or an arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the channel up with one of them, so the water runs straight from the bottom of the picture to the pillars.
card.best_time: Outdoors, early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the cubes. Check the official site before you go for current access and booking.
card.selfie_here: Try the water feature directly in front of the Imam Al Tayeb Mosque: use the front camera, touch the water and let the mosque sit behind you. Or stand outside St Francis Church with your back against its tall columns, with zoom 0.5x to fit more of the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the rooftop garden above The Forum, while you pose in front of the buildings below them.
card.rules_and_safety: Rules can vary from one part of the site to another, so be ready to be asked to stop. Keep your flash off and don't photograph people who are praying. Dress modestly and respect any signs.
card.challenge: Find the mosque's seven arches and get all seven in one frame without a single stranger in it.
card.good_to_know: The Abrahamic Family House is three houses of worship on Saadiyat Island: the Imam Al-Tayeb Mosque, St. Francis Church and the Moses Ben Maimon Synagogue. They opened together on 16 February 2023. Architect David Adjaye made each one a 30-metre cube, set at different angles on a shared plinth.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in The Forum, right beside the water channel that runs across the floor. Face along the channel towards the timber pillars of the church.

card.hook: Most skylines make you pick between the towers and the fun stuff. On the Corniche you get the curving lawn, the fountains and the whole city standing behind them, all in one picture.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of Etihad Towers at the western end of the Corniche, and face the arch between the two towers. The long sweep of the Corniche runs away to the north-east from there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the arch, promenade and fountains all squeeze in. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the towers. From the Marina Breakwater or the Heritage Village pier, try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull the skyline closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and centre the gap between the towers so the arch becomes a frame, then tap the sky or the bright towers and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon light is best. In summer the heat is strong, so early morning or after 5 PM is kinder to you and your phone.
card.selfie_here: Step into the archway between the Etihad Towers at the western end, a signature frame that looks best in late afternoon light. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low so the towers rise over your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, try the tip of the Breakwater next to the flagpole, where there's a wide open view of the skyline and water.
card.rules_and_safety: The Corniche is free to walk, but check the official site for any restrictions on individual areas. Follow any lifeguard or safety signs along the beach.
card.challenge: Catch the arch, the fountains and one passing cyclist in the same frame, and give yourself bonus points if nobody is wobbling.
card.good_to_know: The Corniche is an 8-kilometre promenade along the western side of Abu Dhabi's main island. It was extended onto reclaimed land between 2002 and 2004. Before the 1970s this was a beach where dhows and ships anchored to unload cargo and passengers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in front of Etihad Towers at the western end of the Corniche, and face the arch between the two towers. The long sweep of the Corniche runs away to the north-east from there.

card.hook: Here's a bridge secret: the best view of Sheikh Zayed Bridge is from the water's edge, not from the bridge. From there the arches sweep across your screen like a giant wave.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public waterfront promenade next to the Fairmont Bab Al Bahr hotel. Face north-west, where the full length of the bridge's arches runs across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole span in. Try 0.5x if you're close or want more water in front, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of a few arches and their reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the water's edge up with a horizontal line, so the horizon stays straight and the arches sit in the upper third.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, or just after, when the bridge lights come on and the arches reflect on the water. The reflections can look quite different from one minute to the next, so take a few shots as the light changes.
card.selfie_here: Try the waterfront promenade at The Souk at Qaryat Al Beri. One guide calls it one of the cleaner views, with the arches framed and water rather than traffic nearby. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the arches over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the waterfront by the Fairmont Bab Al Bahr hotel and ask them to take a wide shot with you in front and the arches stretching away behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is a live highway, so please don't stop or take photos on it. Stay on the public waterfront. If you plan to fly a drone, check the current rules with the local authorities.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the arches and their reflection look like a matching pair, with the water line dead level on your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Sheikh Zayed Bridge is a long road bridge with a run of sweeping arches. Maqta Fort (also called Al Maqta'a Museum, so check the name on the day) is said to show the bridge beside the old Maqta crossing. That makes it a good place to compare the older route with the newer structure.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public waterfront promenade next to the Fairmont Bab Al Bahr hotel. Face north-west, where the full length of the bridge's arches runs across the water.

card.hook: Two slim towers, one taller than the other, with a little bridge stitched between them like a handle. That's Nation Towers, and it looks good even on a tiny phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand on Corniche Road, near the southern end of the Corniche. Face south-west, because that's where the towers rise over the waterfront boulevard, with the Gulf and the walkways in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and the waterfront in one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the skybridge near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand straight, and keep a strip of walkway or water at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light and fewer harsh reflections off the glass. Dusk is worth a try too if you switch on night mode and rest your phone against a railing or wall.
card.selfie_here: Try Bainunah Park on the Corniche: stand in the park's greenery with the towers behind you, using the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front). A photo-spot guide says the park's greenery makes the towers stand out on their own, though it describes a building shot rather than a selfie, so check the angle on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on the Corniche road directly across from the towers, near the Nation Riviera Beach Club, to frame the whole complex behind you.
card.challenge: Get both towers and the skybridge in one shot, then see if you can spot the bridge in your photo without zooming in.
card.good_to_know: The towers were completed in 2013 and have 65 and 52 floors. They hold apartments, offices, a shopping mall and the St. Regis hotel. The skybridge, about 202.5 metres up and joining floors 50 and 54, was the highest in the world when it was finished.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Corniche Road, near the southern end of the Corniche. Face south-west, because that's where the towers rise over the waterfront boulevard, with the Gulf and the walkways in view.

card.hook: Picture a palm-frond hut with a glass tower poking up behind it, like the city is peeking over the fence. That's Heritage Village, and it's often quieter than the busy waterfront too.
card.stand_here: Walk in among the tents and palm-frond huts until you reach the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the subject. Face the huts and keep the tall towers behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the huts and towers in one frame. Try zoom 0.5x for a close, low shot of a hut with sky above, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to make the towers look bigger behind the huts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the huts on the lower line and the towers along the upper one, then tap the tents and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the golden light gives the tents, huts and palm fronds warm tones. Opening days and hours change during Ramadan and holidays, so check before you go.
card.selfie_here: A visitor took a two-person selfie just inside the entrance gate, next to the small structure with ducks where water pours from a pot. Use the front camera and try 0.5x, but check your screen, because the village may not end up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the brick entrance arch that carries the village name, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing people, and always ask craftspeople before shooting them at work. Drones are typically restricted here, so stick to phone shots.
card.challenge: Get the lowest hut in the bottom third and the smallest tower in the top third, with nobody's thumb in the corner.
card.good_to_know: Heritage Village has traditional Bedouin tents and palm-frond huts. The contrast with the city towers shows old and new Abu Dhabi in one frame. For another view, Heritage Village Beach has wooden dhows and a sandy shore with the skyline across the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk in among the tents and palm-frond huts until you reach the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the subject. Face the huts and keep the tall towers behind them.

card.hook: Picture a glass tower wearing about 2,000 umbrella-shaped panels that open and close with the sun. That's Al Bahr Towers, and yes, they're as fun to look at as they sound.
card.stand_here: Head to Al Saada Street, near the junction with Al Salam Street, where the twin towers come into view. From the map spot it's roughly 10 minutes on foot to the towers, and they're to the east, so face east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and some sky. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tall edges of the towers up with the vertical lines so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Sunset light is often praised, and the panels move with the sun, so a morning shot can look quite different from a sunset one. Try more than one time if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try Al Gurm on the Corniche, which looks across the water at the towers. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the towers over your shoulder, but expect them to look smaller from that far away.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Al Saada Street near the Al Salam Street junction to take your photo, with you standing with the towers behind you and them facing you.
card.rules_and_safety: These are working offices, so enjoy the towers from the public street rather than expecting to wander around them.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of both towers, then one close-up of the panel pattern, and see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: The panel pattern is inspired by the mashrabiya, the wooden lattice screens used in traditional Arabic buildings. One tower is the headquarters of the Abu Dhabi Investment Council, and the other is the head office of Al Hilal Bank. Both rise 29 storeys, about 145 m.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Al Saada Street, near the junction with Al Salam Street, where the twin towers come into view. From the map spot it's roughly 10 minutes on foot to the towers, and they're to the east, so face east.

The Wikimedia photo of a fountain with the towers behind has camera coordinates (about 24.4529, 54.4063) but no name for the fountain, so I left it out. The Tripadvisor Bab al Bahr piers face the Grand Canal and the mosque rather than the towers, so I left them out too.
